title: Why chemists analyse substances

draft.title: Why chemists analyse substances
card: analysis finds out what is in a substance. It answers the question: which substances or ions are present?
analysis finds out how much of a substance is present, such as a mass or a concentration.
Water suppliers test for harmful metals and bacteria. Food makers check for contaminants and for ingredients that must be listed on labels.
Miners analyse ore to see which metals it holds and how much, so they can judge if mining it is worthwhile. Doctors test blood and urine to help diagnose illness and check treatment.
draft.remember: Analysis answers two questions: what is there, and how much of it is there.

a.q: A lab tests a river sample and reports that it contains 0.8 mg/L of lead. What does this result show?
opts: What is present and how much of it
Only that the water is unsafe to drink
Only how pure the whole sample is
a.why: Naming lead says what is present, and 0.8 mg/L says how much. A result with both is qualitative and quantitative. It does not say the water is unsafe by itself, because that needs a comparison with a safe limit.
a.clue: Look for both a name and an amount in the result.

b.q: A mining company drills a new site. A chemist first finds that the rock contains copper, then measures the percentage of copper in it. Which describes these two steps in order?
b.why: Finding that copper is present answers what is there, so it is qualitative. Measuring the percentage answers how much, so it is quantitative. Reversing them is tempting, but an amount cannot be measured until you know which substance to measure.
b.clue: One step names the substance. The other gives an amount.

a.best: What is present and how much of it
